The comparison is valid on this evidence as a qualitative comparison of earnings models, but it is not a same-basis numeric comparison because the firms use different revenue definitions, units, periods, and scopes. The driver of the difference is that Schwab's direct-to-investor brokerage and bank earns predominantly through the cash-spread (net interest) model on client cash, while the advisor-led models earn predominantly through asset-based fees on client assets. Schwab's 2025 10-K reports net interest revenue of $11.8 billion within $23.9 billion of total net revenues in 2025 and states client cash is a significant funding source; trade-press reporting attributes Schwab's model to the cash-spread business model, reports net interest revenues were 49.3% of Schwab's 2025 revenues, and reports only 5% of Schwab retail households are in fee-based advice. In contrast, the advisor-led firms describe asset-based fees as the core of their earnings on client assets: Morgan Stanley's 10-K states asset management revenues are generally based on the net asset value of the account; Edward Jones' 10-K states fee revenue is composed of asset-based fees based on the average daily market value of client assets plus account and activity fees; Raymond James' 10-K states the Private Client Group generally charges asset-based fees or sales commissions; and Bank of America's CFO stated GWIM is primarily a fee-based advice-driven model with about 30% of revenue as net interest income. Morgan Stanley also states that any revenues earned by Wealth Management on client assets will vary depending upon the services and products provided.
